newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Safeguards needed to protect HK law and order-party.
newsitem.headline: Safeguards needed to protect HK law and order-party.

text.p: One of the largest pro-Beijing political parties in Hong Kong threw its support on Wednesday behind China's plans to dilute civil liberties in the territory -- but also proposed some compromise safeguards.

The safeguards suggested by the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB) -- the largest of the pro-Beijing parties in the legislature -- may blunt, but are unlikely to fundamentally alter, the impact of the changes proposed by China and endorsed by Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa.
The party said in a statement it supported the thrust of the changes to balance freedoms with the need to preserve law and order.

Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp, the British administration and its allies in the West oppose the proposed changes which they argue will erode freedoms and civil liberties in the wealthy territory of 6.4 million people when the British colony reverts to China later this year.
The changes centre on curbing street protests and banning foreign funding of political groups after the handover at midnight on June 30, 1997.

The DAB, which draws much of its support from China-funded neighbourhood organisations and grassroot bodies, sought to reduce the notice period for applying for permission to stage demonstrations to 48 hours in exceptional cases.
Tung supports plans to require protest organisers to seek police permission to demonstrate seven days in advance.
At present, demonstrators are required to notify the police of their plans -- but do not have to seek permission.
The DAB also urged Tung to insert specific phrases in his proposed legislative changes to guard against arbitrary controls.

The laws should "...also include the phrase that 'no restrictions may be placed on the exercise of this right of (preaceful assembly) other than those imposed in conformity with the law and which are necessary in the interests of a democratic society," the DAB statement said.
It said the wording on the ban on funding should be amended to "organisations based outside Hong Kong" instead of "foreign organisations or aliens."

The DAB has been awarded 10 seats in the 60-member provisional legislature established to replace the present elected chamber, which was returned in 1995 under the auspices of British democratic reforms that outraged Beijing.

The pro-business pro-China Liberal Party also occupies 10 seats in the 60-seat provisional legislature which is expected to serve for about a year until new elections under yet-to-be drafted electoral laws are held.

The pro-democracy lobby has boycotted the provisional legislature, selected in December, on the grounds the body is unconstitutional and argues its establishment has seriously undermined political freedom in Hong Kong.
